query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In nanoscale FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy multilayers under sustained loading, progressive plastic (creep) deformation is primarily governed by interface-mediated mechanisms. Specifically, intentionally increasing interfacial lattice distortions and compositional gradients promotes localized enhanced diffusion and dislocation climb, thereby accelerating creep relative to multilayers with more homogeneous interfaces.
generation.material_initial_state: FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy multilayers with nanoscale layers exhibiting inherent lattice distortions and local short-range order at the interfaces.
generation.intervention: Systematic adjustment of interface chemistry via compositional tuning and variation of layer thickness to modulate the degree of lattice distortion and short-range order.
generation.conditions: Sustained mechanical loading under controlled stress levels and temperatures that are sufficient to activate diffusion and dislocation climb processes.
generation.structural_mediator: The interfacial regions characterized by engineered compositional gradients, pronounced lattice distortion, and altered short-range order.
generation.mechanism: An interplay between bulk dislocation glide and interface-localized deformation processes—specifically, enhanced atomic diffusion or dislocation climb facilitated by severe lattice distortions at chemically complex interfaces—which together lower the barrier to creep deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline multilayer with homogeneous interface chemistry, samples with higher interface distortions are expected to exhibit earlier onset of creep, increased strain localization at interfaces, and overall higher creep strain rates under sustained loading.
generation.baseline: FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy multilayers with relatively uniform, less distorted interface chemistry.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate in multilayers retaining nanoscale architecture under sustained loading at temperatures where diffusion processes become activated; effects might be negligible if the interfacial distortions do not exceed a critical threshold.
generation.uncertainty: The relative quantitative contributions of enhanced diffusion versus dislocation climb at the modified interfaces remain uncertain, and precise thresholds for the onset of interface-driven creep require further calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy multilayers: one set with intentionally enhanced interface chemical gradients and lattice distortions via compositional tuning and reduced layer thickness, and a control set with homogeneous interface chemistry. Subject both sets to identical sustained load creep tests under controlled temperature and stress conditions while monitoring microstructural evolution in situ (e.g., using transmission electron microscopy).
measurements: Onset of localized strain accumulation at interfaces (via in situ imaging)
Dislocation density and mobility measurements near interfaces
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant earlier creep onset, increased interface-localized strain consolidation, or higher creep strain rates compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis that interfacial modifications drive creep via enhanced diffusion/dislocation climb is falsified.

High or medium- entropy alloys (HEAs/MEAs) are multi-principal element alloys with equal atomic elemental composition, some of which have shown record-breaking mechanical performance. However, the link between short-range order (SRO) and the exceptional mechanical properties of these alloys has remained elusive. The local destruction of SRO by dislocation glide has been predicted to lead to a rejuvenated state with increased entropy and free energy, creating softer zones within the matrix and planar fault boundaries that enhance the ductility, but this has not been verified. Here, we integrate in situ nanomechanical testing with energy-filtered four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D-STEM) and directly observe the rejuvenation during cyclic mechanical loading in single crystal CrCoNi at room temperature. Surprisingly, stacking faults (SFs) and twin boundaries (TBs) are reversible in initial cycles but become irreversible after a thousand cycles, indicating SF energy reduction and rejuvenation. The mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys are receiving continuous attention as they combine excellent strength with ductility,. One of the microscopic origins of their features lies in the slow dislocation activity in these alloys, that is caused by the lattice distortion brought about by the mix of atomic constituents with various sizes. Recently, high-entropy alloys forming single-phase bcc crystals have come into the focus of research. Among them, the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy has become one of the best investigated examples; it is also known as the Senkov alloy. Thus, Xu et al. directly model the shear strength of the HfNbTaTiZr alloy and observe failure by a bcc-to-fcc phase transformation initiating in HfTi rich regions. Liang et al. study how variable fractions of Hf and Ta in HfNbTaTiZr alloys affect the tensile strength. Recently, Hf15Nb40Ta25Ti15Zr15 was found to be both strong and ductile at cryogenic to elevated temperatures. In this paper, MD simulations are conducted to systematically investigate the creep behavior of HESAs under varying stress, temperature, γ/γ′ lattice misfit, and γ′ volume fraction. The creep mechanism and the critical creep resistance factors are explored. The main conclusions are summarized as follows: The creep behavior of both HESAs and HEAs is strongly influenced by stress and temperature, and their combined effect governs the rate of atomic rearrangement during deformation. As these parameters increase, the creep rate accelerates rapidly due to enhanced diffusion and easier activation of deformation carriers. Temperature plays a particularly dominant role, as high thermal energy significantly facilitates atomic mobility, vacancy migration, and interface-mediated processes. Compared with HEAs, HESAs consistently exhibit lower creep strain under identical conditions, and the difference becomes more pronounced at higher stress–temperature combinations, highlighting the intrinsic microstructural advantages of γ/γ′-strengthened systems.

frame.system: FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers that form a nanoscale multilayer coating with complex composition, severe lattice distortions, and potential short-range order in the individual layers.
frame.goal: To establish a testable mechanistic hypothesis that explains the progressive plastic (creep) deformation under sustained loading, identifying what internal features govern the deformation response in these complex multilayer systems.
frame.limitation: Conventional deformation models developed for simpler metallic multilayers do not necessarily apply because high-entropy alloys exhibit compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order. Additionally, prior preliminary evidence in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers has been insufficient to clearly define when and how different deformation responses (e.g., dislocation glide, diffusion-controlled creep) dominate.
root_cause_cues: insufficient to establish what controls creep
constraints: must retain a nanoscale multilayer coating architecture
a balance is required between high strength and deformation tolerance (ductility/resilience under sustained load)
frame.regime: Sustained loading conditions (i.e., creep conditions) where time-dependent, progressive plastic deformation dominates, potentially at elevated temperatures where diffusion or dislocation climb could be activated.
prior_attempts: Conventional metallic multilayer studies provided a framework for deformation but assumed simpler compositions and lattice structures which do not translate directly to high-entropy systems.

Preliminary investigations on FCC/BCC high-entropy multilayers have not clearly isolated the controlling mechanism, leaving ambiguity over whether dislocation-mediated processes, diffusion-assisted creep, or interface/boundary effects are dominant.
frame.understanding: A promising hypothesis is that under sustained loading, the progressive plastic deformation in high-entropy-alloy multilayers is governed by an interplay between dislocation activity and diffusion-mediated processes localized at the interfaces. Specifically, the severe lattice distortions and short-range order in the individual layers could promote a localized concentration of strain at the interfaces, facilitating either stress-driven chemical diffusion or enhanced dislocation climb. A controlled comparison of structures with varying interface chemistries, degrees of lattice distortion (by adjusting alloy composition or processing parameters), and layer thickness could expose this behavior. It is predicted that relative to a baseline with less distorted interfaces, samples with higher compositional gradients and distortion will exhibit earlier onset of creep deformation, more pronounced strain localization at interfaces, and perhaps distinct microstructural evolution under continuous loading. Boundary conditions such as stress magnitude, temperature, and layer thickness should be systematically varied. Prior support comes from analogous studies in simpler multilayer systems where interface-mediated mechanisms were identified, as well as from theoretical models predicting enhanced diffusivity and dislocation activity in highly distorted lattices. A result that falsifies the hypothesis would be the observation that adjusting interface chemistry and lattice distortion parameters does not appreciably shift the creep response or the activation of deformation modes, thereby suggesting that factors other than the proposed interplay (such as bulk diffusion or other mechanisms) control the progressive plastic deformation.

decision.trend: Earlier studies in high‐entropy alloys began by identifying dislocation‐mediated mechanisms in relatively simpler, ordered or two‐phase systems (as in PMC4949441), establishing the importance of dislocation structure on strength. Subsequent work (PMC12842692) extended the focus to time‐dependent, creep-like conditions in high-entropy superalloys, where factors such as lattice misfit, phase morphology, and temperature were shown to affect the competition between atomic diffusion and dislocation-based deformation. More recent investigations (PMC10873362) have highlighted how strain‐induced breakdown of short‐range order at interfaces can modify local plasticity. Despite these advances, the specific role of nanoscale interfaces in FCC/BCC high-entropy multilayers—especially how severe lattice distortions and local chemical order at the interfaces modulate the transition from dislocation glide to diffusion-assisted creep—remains unsolved.
decision.unsolved: It is still unclear how the unique interfacial environments in nanoscale FCC/BCC high-entropy multilayers, characterized by compositional complexity, severe lattice distortions, and potentially strong short-range order, govern the progressive plastic (creep) deformation. In particular, the interplay between localized diffusion (e.g., stress-driven chemical diffusion or dislocation climb) and dislocation activity at these distorted interfaces under sustained load remains to be delineated.
decision.lever: Systematically adjusting interface chemistry (via compositional tuning at the interfaces) and layer thickness to modulate the degree of lattice distortion and local short-range order, while performing in situ sustained-load (creep) tests
decision.why: This approach directly follows the trend of isolating key mechanistic factors. Prior work has separately linked dislocation-dominated deformation and diffusion-assisted processes to lattice distortions and SRO; by controlling these interfacial parameters in multilayer coatings, the experiment can expose how subtle changes in local chemistry and structure trigger a shift from dislocation glide to enhanced diffusion or dislocation climb, thereby testing the hypothesis regarding interfacial control of progressive plastic deformation.
